title: Teaching & Mentoring
section: Courses I Am Interested in Teaching
text:
Courses I Am Interested in Teaching
My interdisciplinary background in industrial engineering, transportation research, and applied climate-risk planning positions me to contribute to undergraduate and graduate courses in urban transportation and accessibility, geographic information systems (GIS) and spatial analysis, climate risk and infrastructure resilience, engineering economics, decision analysis, and sustainable urban systems. I am particularly interested in teaching courses that connect quantitative and computational methods with questions of equity, sustainability, and environmental planning.
Across these areas, my teaching approach emphasizes connecting analytical methods to real-world challenges. I aim to help students develop strong technical foundations while critically examining the assumptions, uncertainties, and societal implications of the tools they use. I am also interested in developing interdisciplinary courses that bridge infrastructure systems, urban planning, and community-centered decision-making.

title: Teaching & Mentoring
text:
Mentorship
I view mentorship as an opportunity to help students develop not only technical expertise but also intellectual independence, critical thinking, and an appreciation for the broader societal implications of their research. My experience mentoring undergraduate and graduate researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds has reinforced the importance of adapting guidance to students’ individual interests, experiences, and professional goals.
My mentoring approach emphasizes collaborative learning, progressive independence, and meaningful engagement with research problems. I aim to create an environment where students feel comfortable exploring new methods, questioning assumptions, and contributing their own perspectives. Through interdisciplinary and applied research opportunities, I hope to support students in developing the analytical, communication, and collaborative skills necessary to address complex challenges in academia, industry, and public service.

title: Research
text: My research develops systems-based, data-driven, and community-informed approaches to understand how infrastructure shapes everyday opportunities and how communities experience environmental and infrastructure disruption. Three research directions connect my work.

title: Research
section: Critical and Essential-service Access and Community Resilience
text:
Critical and Essential-service Access and Community Resilience
Who can access critical and essential services, how fragile is that access, and how can we make it more resilient?
My research examines how transportation and infrastructure systems shape people’s ability to access critical and essential services (CES), including health care, education, and emergency services. Moving beyond traditional measures of facility availability and proximity, I develop accessibility-based approaches to assess whether populations can reach essential services, what alternatives are available to them, and how vulnerable that access may be to infrastructure disruptions and natural hazards.
In Evaluating critical and essential service access vulnerabilities, my coauthors and I co-developed measures of service-access fragility, facility criticality, and equity with community members who attended our workshops. Building on this foundation, my ongoing research examines geographic and sociodemographic disparities in access to essential services across the United States, including differences in health-care accessibility and their implications for population well-being. I am also extending these approaches to evaluate how coastal hazards, infrastructure disruptions, and climate adaptation strategies affect communities’ ability to maintain access to essential services over time.

Building on this foundation, three nationwide studies currently in preparation for publication examine complementary dimensions of access to critical and essential services: (1) geographic and demographic disparities in health-care access and their implications for health outcomes; (2) regional differences in essential-service accessibility, access fragility, and facility criticality; and (3) distributional inequities in essential-service access across sociodemographic groups.
I am also extending these approaches to evaluate how coastal hazards, infrastructure disruptions, and climate adaptation strategies affect communities’ ability to maintain access to essential services over time.

title: Research
section: Robust Decision-Making for Infrastructure and Climate Adaptation
text:
Robust Decision-Making for Infrastructure and Climate Adaptation
Which infrastructure investments remain effective across uncertain futures and divergent stakeholder priorities?
My research develops decision-support approaches to identify infrastructure and climate-adaptation strategies that remain effective across uncertain futures and divergent stakeholder priorities. I combine multi-criteria decision analysis with robustness analysis to examine how infrastructure investment priorities change under different assumptions and competing objectives. Rather than requiring agreement on a single set of subjective weights, these approaches identify priorities that remain stable across alternative decision perspectives, helping planners make more transparent and defensible decisions.
Through my professional work at Arcadis, I have applied these approaches to statewide transportation flood-risk assessment and infrastructure prioritization. These experiences inform my broader research on bridging methodological advances with the institutional constraints, uncertainties, and practical challenges of infrastructure and climate-adaptation planning.

Project status (as of October 20, 2026): The applied project described above has not been publicly released. The identity of the state transportation agency and project-specific details remain confidential. Relevant files will be shared once the project is released to public.

title: Research
text:
Community-Informed Infrastructure Prioritization
Which critical and essential services should be prioritized for protection, and how can community preferences inform these decisions?


Infrastructure risk-mitigation decisions often rely on engineering and economic measures that do not fully capture what communities consider important to protect. My research examines how residents prioritize critical and essential services, how these preferences vary across individuals, and how community priorities can be incorporated into infrastructure investment decisions alongside conventional risk measures.
In my doctoral research on seismic risk mitigation, I use Best-Worst Scaling and discrete-choice modeling to elicit residents’ preferences for protecting essential-service facilities in Los Angeles. I integrate these findings into multi-criteria decision-support frameworks to examine how community priorities can inform seismic retrofit prioritization.
Beyond seismic risk, I aim to develop transferable approaches that enable communities to shape the objectives and tradeoffs used in infrastructure and climate-adaptation planning. This work emphasizes community engagement as a collaborative process in which local knowledge informs not only the evaluation of potential interventions, but also how planning problems are defined.





Community preferences for seismic retrofit prioritization



Points indicate the estimated rank of each service based on its multinomial logit coefficient, with Rank 1 representing the highest-priority service. Vertical bars show the range of ranks that cannot be statistically distinguished based on pairwise coefficient-difference tests.

title: Research
text:
Equitable Mobility and Sustainability Transitions
How can transitions toward sustainable transportation expand mobility opportunities without creating new inequities?


My transportation research examines how mobility opportunities, infrastructure investments, and sustainability transitions distribute benefits and burdens across communities.
In my master’s research, I developed a capabilities-based framework for transportation equity that considers individuals’ actual travel needs and the feasibility of alternative transportation modes. Using GPS-based travel behavior data, this work moves beyond the geographic availability of transportation options to examine whether individuals have realistic alternatives for meeting their daily mobility needs. An associated manuscript on mode choice and mobility-option equity is currently in preparation.
My subsequent research examines the transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and its implications for urban equity. In a published study, my coauthors and I investigated the role of the built environment in EV adoption. Building on this work, my ongoing research examines whether EV charging infrastructure investments, despite their environmental benefits, may contribute to unintended pressures on housing affordability and exacerbate existing urban inequalities.
A complementary direction of my research investigates rebound and tertiary effects associated with sustainability transitions. This includes system dynamics modeling of behavioral and economic responses to energy savings, as well as research on how corporations disclose the indirect consequences of their sustainability initiatives.

title: Utkuhan Genc
text:
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering at Purdue University, advised by Professor David R. Johnson, and a Climate Risk Specialist at Arcadis. My research examines how changes in urban and infrastructure systems shape access to critical and essential services (CES) and opportunities, how climate and natural hazards compound existing disparities, and how planners can incorporate community priorities and deep uncertainty into consequential decisions.
My research lies at the intersection of urban mobility, infrastructure resilience, community-centered climate adaptation, and equitable planning. I combine computational and geospatial modeling, transportation-network analysis, systems modeling, risk and decision science, and community-engaged research to understand how regional and environmental change affect communities and translate these insights into equitable, resilient, and community-informed planning decisions.
A central part of my research studies access to critical and essential services. In published work on service-access vulnerabilities, my coauthors and I examined how limited alternatives to schools, hospitals, and other facilities can make communities vulnerable to disruption. I am extending this work to nationwide accessibility disparities and to the effects of coastal flooding and sea-level rise on community function. Learn more about this research.
I also study transportation equity and the built environment including mobility options beyond the private automobile, the evolving importance of the built environment for electric-vehicle adoption, and potential housing-affordability implications of charging-infrastructure development. Complementary climate mitigation work that focuses on rebound effects examines sustainability reporting and indirect environmental effects.
Across these projects, my research is guided by a central question: How can we plan and adapt urban and infrastructure systems to expand access, reduce inequities, and remain responsive to community priorities under environmental change and uncertainty?
Drawing on interdisciplinary academic collaborations and applied climate-risk practice, I combine computational and systems-based approaches with community knowledge to develop analytical frameworks and decision-support tools that help planners, agencies, and communities make more equitable, resilient, and robust decisions.
For more details, see my research, publications, teaching, and selected talks. You can reach me at ugenc@purdue.edu.

title: Selected Talks
text:
Natural Hazards Research and Applications Workshop, Researchers Meeting, Broomfield, Colorado.
I presented preliminary results from our best-worst scaling survey that was fielded in Los Angeles County among households with less than $100,000 income. The target group was selected because low-income households have fewer opportunities to participate directly in formal decision-making process. We used Best-Worst Scaling with Balanced Incomplete Block Design to quantify priority rankings of 23 different critical and essential services with minimal cognitive burden on respondents. Scores range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating stronger access based on relative drive time to the nearest facility, relative drive time to the second-nearest facility, and the share of the population with at least two facilities within the service-specific critical time threshold.

text:
2025

Integrating Equity and Community Perspectives in Seismic Retrofit Decisions.
Society for Risk Analysis Annual Meeting, Washington, DC.
This presentation introduced the initial, risk-focused version of our seismic retrofit prioritization framework using a case study in Los Angeles. For updated findings and figures, as well as the associated preprint, please refer to the more recent presentation at Natural Hazards Workshop in 2026. View Slides (PDF)


Using Equitable Access to Essential Services as Guidance for Investments in Coastal Adaptation.
Arcadis North America Monthly Seminar Series, San Francisco (invited seminar).
I was invited to give a talk to the Water Resources and Climate Adaptation team at Arcadis’s San Francisco office. In this presentation, I discussed how the fragility of access to critical and essential services can inform social measures of infrastructure criticality and how robustness analysis can support infrastructure prioritization and decision-making. Rather than requiring agreement on a single set of subjective weights, the proposed framework identifies priorities that remain stable across different decision-maker perspectives. View Slides (PDF)
An example visualization of the robustness analysis framework is shown below. Each color represents the ranking assigned to a particular facility under different combinations of weights across three outcome measures. Regions with the same color indicate weighting combinations that produce the same ranking, illustrating how robust the facility’s prioritization is to differences in decision-maker preferences.
